title: Strategic Leadership and Change Management
subtitle: Set direction, turn strategy into unit plans and lead people through mergers, migrations and restructuring
summary: Read Ethiopia's fast-changing financial landscape, cascade strategy into KPIs and lead large change with people on board, using a two-bank merger as the running case.
audience: Branch, department and senior managers in Ethiopian banks, microfinance institutions and other financial firms who already manage people and now lead units, programs or transformations.
objectives: Analyze the strategic environment of Ethiopian finance with PESTEL, five forces and scenarios
Translate strategy into unit-level plans, OKRs and KPIs and review performance against them
Lead large change programs such as mergers, system migrations and restructuring with structured stakeholder management
Build high-performing, inclusive teams and a culture that supports strategy
Make sound, ethical decisions under pressure and present a 12-month change roadmap

runningCase.name: Project Andinet: the Bank A and Bank B merger
runningCase.text: Bank A, an Addis Ababa based commercial bank with 210 branches, 4,300 staff and paid-up capital of Birr 3.4 billion, and Bank B, a regional bank with 95 branches, 1,800 staff and Birr 2.1 billion, have agreed, subject to shareholder and NBE approval, to merge so that the combined bank meets the Birr 5 billion minimum paid-up capital. The boards have named Hirut Alemu, Bank A's head of strategy, to lead a transformation office that must deliver a 12-month change roadmap: one legal entity, one core banking system (Bank A's), one brand and one culture, with 41 towns where both banks have a branch and without losing customers or critical staff. Each module adds a piece of the roadmap, which you present in the capstone.

modules.title: Strategic thinking for Ethiopian finance
modules.summary: Read the forces reshaping Ethiopian finance and turn them into scenarios and clear strategic choices for your unit.
objectives: Explain how a senior leader's job shifts from running operations to setting direction
Apply PESTEL to the post-2024 Ethiopian financial system
Use the five forces to judge competitive pressure on a banking business line
Build scenarios for foreign bank entry, consolidation and digital competition and pick no-regret moves

lessons.title: From running the unit to setting direction
body: Management keeps today's business working: plans, budgets, staffing, controls. Leadership decides where the business should go next and brings people with it. A branch or department manager needs both, but as you move up, a growing share of your time should go to direction, priorities and people rather than to approving transactions.

Two styles matter most at this level. Situational leadership adjusts how much you direct or support each person to their skill and commitment on a given task. Transformational leadership gives people a purpose that is bigger than this quarter's targets, sets an example and challenges them to think. In a period of foreign bank entry, consolidation and digitalization, staff need both: clear direction on the task and a reason to believe in the change.

Ethiopian organizational culture shapes how this works. Respect for hierarchy and age means junior staff often wait for the senior person to speak and rarely disagree in public. Collectivism means people care strongly about the team and about relationships. A strategic leader uses these strengths, loyalty and cohesion, while deliberately inviting challenge: asking juniors to speak first, using small groups and making it safe to bring bad news.

right.title: Leading the unit
items: Sets direction for the next 3 to 5 years

example.title: The department head who spoke last
example.text: Tigist Abebe became head of trade finance at a mid-sized Ethiopian bank after FXD/01/2024 moved the market to freely negotiated exchange rates. In her first strategy meeting nobody disagreed with her plan. She changed the format: each officer wrote down one risk on a card before she spoke, and the most junior person presented first. The team raised three issues she had missed, including exporters asking about the 90-day repatriation rule, and the plan improved.

lessons.tip: In meetings with mixed seniority, ask the most junior person to give their view first.

lessons.title: PESTEL: reading the big picture
body: PESTEL scans six groups of external factors: political and policy, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal. Its value is not the list itself but the question that follows each item: so what does this mean for our customers, our income and our people?

For Ethiopian finance since 2024 the scan is unusually full. The exchange rate is market based under FXD/01/2024. Monetary policy works through the National Bank Rate, which the NBE raised to 16% at MPC meeting No. 7 in July 2026, when it also removed the temporary credit growth cap. Banks set deposit and lending rates freely under NBE/INT/13/2026. The Banking Business Proclamation No. 1360/2025 opens the sector to foreign banks, and the Ethiopian Securities Exchange began in January 2025.
points: Political and policy: the IMF-supported reform program, the Ten Year Development Plan (2021 to 2031) and its sector priorities
Economic: market-based exchange rate, a 16% National Bank Rate, headline inflation reported at 13.4% in May 2026
Social: a young, mobile population and large unbanked groups, especially women and rural households
Technological: Fayda digital ID, mobile wallets and the Digital Ethiopia strategy
Environmental: drought and flood exposure of rain-fed agriculture, which reaches the loan book
Legal: Proclamation No. 1360/2025, licensing under SBB/94/2025 and risk-based capital under SBB/95/2025

items.label: Political and policy
items.text: Reform program, national plans

items.label: Economic
items.text: FX regime, policy rate, inflation

items.label: Social
items.text: Youth, inclusion, trust

items.label: Technological
items.text: Digital ID, wallets, data

items.label: Environmental
items.text: Drought, floods, climate

items.label: Legal
items.text: New banking law and directives

lessons.tip: Finish every PESTEL item with one sentence that starts "For our unit, this means...".

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. FXD/01/2024, Foreign exchange
regulation.text: In force since 29 July 2024, the directive lets banks buy and sell foreign currency at freely negotiated rates, with the NBE publishing only a non-binding indicative rate, and sets rules for export repatriation, import payments, FCY accounts and external loans. Its amendments have since relaxed many approvals. For a strategist it changes FX income, the pricing of trade services and the risks borrowers carry.

lessons.title: Five forces: where the competitive pressure comes from
body: Porter's five forces explain why some business lines earn good returns and others do not. Pressure comes from rivalry among existing players, the threat of new entrants, substitutes, the bargaining power of customers and the bargaining power of suppliers. For a bank, suppliers include depositors (the supplier of funds), skilled staff and technology vendors.

Each force is shifting in Ethiopia. New entrants: SBB/94/2025 sets the licensing path for foreign bank subsidiaries and branches. Substitutes: mobile wallets compete for payments and small balances, and the securities exchange gives large companies a funding route besides bank loans. Customers: with rates set freely, large depositors and corporate borrowers can negotiate harder.

items.label: Rivalry
items.text: Many banks of similar size chase the same customers

items.label: New entrants
items.text: Foreign subsidiaries and branches under the new law

items.label: Substitutes
items.text: Wallets for payments, the exchange for corporate funding

items.label: Customer power
items.text: Large depositors and corporates negotiate freely set rates

items.label: Supplier power
items.text: Depositors, scarce skilled staff, technology vendors

lessons.tip: Score each force high, medium or low for one business line at a time; a whole-bank score hides the differences.

scenario.title: Which force matters most?
scenario.situation: Rahel Mulugeta heads corporate banking at a mid-sized bank. Her ten largest clients are importers and manufacturers. A foreign bank has announced plans for a subsidiary, and two of her clients are preparing bond issues for the exchange.
scenario.question: Which forces should top her strategy review?
options: New entrants and substitutes for corporate funding, which both target her best clients
scenario.explain: A foreign subsidiary and capital market funding both go after the same large corporates. Vendors, MFIs and small savers matter less for this business line.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/94/2025, Licensing and renewal of banking business
regulation.text: In force since 25 June 2025, it sets minimum paid-up capital of Birr 5 billion for a new domestic bank, a foreign bank subsidiary or a foreign bank branch, and USD 100,000 for a representative office. Foreign nationals and foreign-owned Ethiopian organizations may together hold up to 49% of a domestic bank, with a 40% cap for a strategic investor.

lessons.title: Scenario planning: preparing for more than one future
body: A forecast gives one answer and is usually wrong in a period of reform. Scenario planning builds three or four plausible futures from the uncertainties that matter most, then asks which moves work in all of them (no-regret moves), which only pay off in some (options to prepare), and which signals will tell you which future is arriving.

The usual method picks two critical uncertainties that are both important and genuinely uncertain, and crosses them to form four scenarios. For Ethiopian banks, strong candidates are the speed and scale of foreign bank entry, the pace of consolidation among local banks and how fast customers move to digital channels.

items.label: Focal question
items.text: For example: what must our retail business look like in 2030?

items.label: Drivers
items.text: List the PESTEL and five forces items that bear on it

items.label: Two critical uncertainties
items.text: High impact and genuinely uncertain

items.label: Four scenarios
items.text: Name and describe each future in a paragraph

items.label: Signposts
items.text: Early signals that a scenario is arriving

items.label: Moves
items.text: No-regret moves now, options ready for later

example.title: A microfinance institution's two uncertainties
example.text: A microfinance institution in Hawassa ran a half-day workshop. Its leaders chose two uncertainties: how quickly mobile wallets would offer small loans in its villages, and whether rainfall would stay normal. In the worst quadrant, early wallet lending plus drought, the plan was to protect good borrowers with rescheduling. The no-regret move in all four futures was to digitize its own loan collections, which it started that year.

lessons.tip: Give each scenario a memorable name; people remember "Crowded Market" better than "Scenario C".

lessons.title: Running case: Andinet's four futures
body: Hirut Alemu, head of the Andinet transformation office, starts with the environment the merged bank will face. With her strategy team she picks two uncertainties: how fast foreign banks win large corporate and diaspora business, and how fast retail customers move to digital channels.

The four scenarios lead to a short list of no-regret moves for the merged bank: one core banking system, a stronger mobile channel, and protection of the corporate relationships that most competitors will target. These moves become the backbone of the 12-month roadmap you build in this course.

scenario.title: The tempting bet
scenario.situation: Andinet's board chair, Dawit Kebede, believes foreign banks will be slow to arrive. He proposes cutting the mobile banking budget by Birr 120 million and opening 30 new branches instead.
scenario.question: How should Hirut respond?
options: Show that the branch plan only pays off in two quadrants, while mobile investment is a no-regret move, and propose staging branch openings against signposts
Cut both budgets until the merger closes
Agree, since the chair has the most experience
Drop the scenario work and ask for a single forecast
scenario.explain: Scenarios test bets against several futures. Mobile investment works in all four; branch expansion should wait for signposts rather than being ruled in or out now.

worked.title: Andinet scenario matrix

rows.label: Uncertainty 1
rows.value: Foreign banks win large corporates quickly or slowly

rows.label: Uncertainty 2
rows.value: Retail customers go digital quickly or slowly

rows.label: Fast entry, fast digital
rows.value: Crowded Market: margins squeezed, digital is survival

rows.label: Fast entry, slow digital
rows.value: Corporate Battle: defend top clients, branches still matter

rows.label: Slow entry, fast digital
rows.value: Mobile Race: wallets and local rivals are the threat

rows.label: Slow entry, slow digital
rows.value: Breathing Space: time to integrate, but do not relax

rows.label: No-regret moves
rows.value: One core system, strong mobile channel, named relationship managers for the top 200 clients

rows.label: Signposts
rows.value: Foreign licenses granted, wallet transaction growth, corporate deposit share

worked.note: Every quadrant needs a single core banking system and protected corporate relationships, so these go first on the roadmap.

lessons.title: From analysis to strategic choices
body: Analysis is only useful when it ends in choices. Two questions force them: where will we play (customers, regions, products, channels) and how will we win there (price, service, speed, relationships, technology)? A strategy that tries to serve every customer the same way is usually a budget, not a strategy.

A simple test of a unit strategy: can every team member say in one sentence what the unit will do more of, what it will stop doing and how it will measure success? If not, the strategy will be overtaken by daily pressure. Saying no is part of the leader's job.

left.title: Weak strategy statements
items: Be the best bank in Ethiopia

right.title: Strong strategy choices
items: Lead in export and diaspora banking in three corridors
Grow SME lending in five regional cities, exit low-margin consumer lines
Move 60% of transfers to mobile in 18 months

example.title: A regional manager who chose
example.text: Abel Negash manages 22 branches in the Dire Dawa region. Instead of pushing every product, he chose two priorities: trade services for import and export traders and digital onboarding for young customers. He stopped the branch-by-branch competition on consumer loans, which had high arrears. Within a year his fee income rose and arrears fell, and branch staff said for the first time they knew what mattered.

lessons.tip: Write a "stop doing" list next to every strategy; it is often the most useful page.

scenario.title: Matching every competitor
scenario.situation: A competitor launches a diaspora mortgage, a youth account and an agricultural app in the same quarter. Your department head, Fikru Demissie, asks you to copy all three within six months.
scenario.question: What is the best advice?
options: Wait for NBE guidance before acting
Copy all three to avoid losing customers
Test each against your chosen segments and capabilities, pursue the one that fits and decline or defer the others
scenario.explain: Strategy means choosing. Copying everything spreads people and money thin; ignoring rivals is also a mistake. Filter moves through your own choices.

takeaways: At senior level, leadership means setting direction and aligning people, not just running operations well.
Use Ethiopian strengths such as loyalty and cohesion, and deliberately invite challenge from junior staff.
PESTEL and five forces are only useful when each item ends in "so what for our unit".
Foreign entry, consolidation, the market-based exchange rate and digital channels are the key drivers of Ethiopian banking strategy today.
Scenarios replace one forecast with several futures; act now on no-regret moves and watch signposts for the rest.
A real strategy says where to play, how to win and what to stop doing.

quiz.q: Which activity is mainly leadership rather than management?
options: Explaining to staff why the unit will shift from cash services to digital onboarding
quiz.explain: Setting direction and bringing people with you is leadership; the others keep today's operations running.

quiz.q: In which PESTEL group does the move to freely negotiated exchange rates under FXD/01/2024 belong most directly?
options: Economic (and legal as the rule behind it)
quiz.explain: The exchange rate regime is an economic factor created by a legal instrument, the NBE directive.

quiz.q: Under the five forces, depositors are best described as:
options: Suppliers of funds with bargaining power
quiz.explain: Depositors supply the funds a bank lends; with rates set freely they can negotiate.

quiz.q: What makes an uncertainty "critical" for scenario planning?
options: It has high impact and its outcome is genuinely uncertain
It is mentioned in the newspaper
quiz.explain: Critical uncertainties are both important and unpredictable, which is why they define the scenarios.

quiz.q: A no-regret move is one that:
options: Pays off in only one scenario
quiz.explain: No-regret moves are worth doing whichever future arrives.

quiz.q: Under SBB/94/2025, what is the minimum paid-up capital for a foreign bank subsidiary?
quiz.explain: The directive sets Birr 5 billion for each type of bank; USD 100,000 applies to representative offices.

modules.title: Strategy execution: from plan to unit KPIs
modules.summary: Translate strategy into scorecards, OKRs and cascaded targets, and run reviews that change what people do.
objectives: Explain the most common reasons strategies fail in execution
Build a balanced scorecard and write OKRs for a unit
Cascade a bank-level target into fair regional and branch targets
Run performance reviews that are honest, respectful and lead to action

lessons.title: Why good strategies fail in execution
body: Most strategies do not fail because the analysis was wrong. They fail because priorities are unclear, too many initiatives compete for the same people, budgets are set separately from strategy, targets do not reach the front line and nobody reviews progress on a fixed rhythm.

In a bank, the symptom is familiar: a five-year strategy document approved by the board, and branch staff still measured only on deposits and loans. The leader's job is to close that gap, so that every unit and every person can see how their work links to the strategy.
points: Too many priorities: more than five at once usually means none
Budget and headcount not linked to priorities
Targets that stop at head office
Reviews that discuss numbers but agree no actions

example.title: The strategy nobody had read
example.text: A mid-sized bank's new strategy put digital channels and SME lending first. Six months later, Kidist Worku, a new branch manager in Bahir Dar, asked her team what the strategy said. Nobody knew. Their scorecard still had deposits at 70% weight. She rebuilt the branch plan around the two priorities and asked the regional office to change the weights, which it did the next quarter.

lessons.tip: Ask three front-line staff to explain the strategy; their answers tell you whether it has been executed or only published.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/91/2024, Bank corporate governance
regulation.text: In force since 12 June 2024, it requires at least nine directors, one-third of them independent and at least two women, sets a six-year limit on consecutive service and requires four board committees, with NBE approval of the chief risk officer. In practice the board approves strategy and holds management to account for executing it, so unit plans and KPIs are the evidence that strategy is being carried out.

lessons.title: The balanced scorecard
body: Kaplan and Norton's balanced scorecard measures performance from four perspectives: financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth. Financial results are lagging; the other three are leading indicators that explain whether future financial results will come.

A strategy map links objectives across the four: trained staff (learning) run faster onboarding (process), which wins and keeps customers (customer), which grows fee income and deposits (financial). Keep each perspective to two to four objectives, each with one or two measures.

items.label: Financial
items.text: Deposit growth, fee income, cost to income, NPL ratio

items.label: Customer
items.text: New active customers, complaints resolved, digital adoption

items.label: Internal process
items.text: Account opening time, loan turnaround, audit findings closed

items.label: Learning and growth
items.text: Staff trained, key roles filled, engagement score

example.title: A scorecard for a digital banking unit
example.text: Henok Ayele leads a digital banking unit of 18 people. His old report showed only wallet transaction value. His new scorecard adds active users (customer), app crash rate and complaint resolution time (process) and certified staff (learning). In the first review, the team saw that transaction value was rising while active users were flat: a few heavy users drove the growth. They changed their campaign to target new users.

scenario.title: A scorecard with only one perspective
scenario.situation: A branch scorecard has 10 measures: deposits, loans, fee income, interest income, cost, profit, NPL ratio, recoveries, FX income and cash surplus.
scenario.question: What is the main weakness?
options: Fee income is not a valid measure
It measures only financial results, so it gives no early warning on customers, processes or people
scenario.explain: All ten are financial and lagging. A balanced scorecard adds customer, process and learning measures that predict future results.

lessons.title: OKRs: objectives and key results
body: OKRs are a simple way to focus a team for a quarter. The objective is qualitative and inspiring: what we want to achieve. Key results, usually two to four, are measurable outcomes that prove the objective was met. Initiatives, the tasks you do, are listed separately.

Good key results measure outcomes, not activity. "Hold 20 training sessions" is an activity; "80% of account openings done on tablet by June" is a result. OKRs suit change programs because they focus a team on a few things for a short period, while the scorecard tracks the steady business.

visual.caption: Initiatives are the work; key results are the evidence that the work changed something.

example.title: Tablet account opening as an OKR
example.text: Mahlet Fikre, a branch manager in Adama, set this OKR for her branch: Objective, make account opening fast and paperless. Key results: 85% of new accounts opened on tablet by the end of the quarter; average opening time below 15 minutes; zero accounts returned by the back office for missing KYC fields. Her initiatives were daily practice for tellers, a floor walker at peak hours and a weekly review of returned files.

scenario.title: Rewrite the key result
scenario.situation: A department's OKR reads: Objective, improve SME lending. Key result: hold 12 meetings with SME associations.
scenario.question: Which key result is best?
options: Approve 150 new SME loans with average turnaround under 10 working days and arrears below the bank's target
scenario.explain: A key result measures an outcome. Meetings, brochures and visits are activities that may or may not produce results.

lessons.title: Cascading targets to regions and branches
body: Cascading turns a bank-level target into targets for regions, branches and individuals. A fair cascade uses each unit's potential (market size, customer base, staff, history) rather than splitting the total evenly or simply adding a percentage to last year.

Agree targets with unit heads rather than only sending them down. Managers who help set targets own them; managers who receive an unexplained number find reasons why it cannot be met. Keep the link visible: every branch target should add up to the regional target, and every regional target to the bank's.

visual.caption: Regional shares of a Birr 6,000 million target, from the worked example.

lessons.tip: Publish the method behind the cascade, not only the numbers; transparency reduces arguments.

worked.title: Cascading a Birr 6 billion deposit growth target (worked example)

rows.label: Addis Ababa region: 45% of deposit potential
Hawassa branch: 9% of South region potential

worked.note: Potential-based shares are fairer than equal splits, and the check that the parts add up to the whole keeps the cascade honest.

lessons.title: Running case: a scorecard for a merged branch
body: In Andinet, 41 towns have both a Bank A and a Bank B branch. Where two branches combine, the manager needs a scorecard that rewards keeping customers through the merger, not only growth. Hirut's team designs a weighted scorecard for the first year after integration.

Weights show what matters. Customer retention gets the highest weight because losing customers during a merger is the biggest risk. The scorecard is scored as actual divided by target, capped at 120% so that one measure cannot hide a failure on another.

scenario.title: A score that hides a problem
scenario.situation: Another merged branch scores 104 overall: deposit growth is 150% of target (capped at 120%), but customer retention is 85% against 95%.
scenario.question: What should the regional manager do?
options: Congratulate the branch on its score
Raise next year's deposit target only
Recognize the deposit result but treat the retention gap as the priority, and ask the manager for a recovery plan
scenario.explain: Retention carries the highest weight because it is the main merger risk. A strong number elsewhere should not hide it.

worked.title: Hawassa merged branch, first-year scorecard

rows.label: Deposit growth: target Birr 97.2m, actual Birr 104m (weight 20%)
Accounts migrated without error: target 99%, actual 97% (weight 20%)
Staff completing integration training: target 100%, actual 80% (weight 15%)

worked.note: The total looks fine, but training at 80% and retention below target are the two issues the manager must act on.

lessons.title: Performance reviews that change behavior
body: Reviews turn a scorecard into action. A useful rhythm is a short weekly team huddle, a monthly one-to-one with each direct report and a quarterly review of the unit scorecard with your own manager. Each review ends with agreed actions, owners and dates.

In Ethiopian workplaces, public criticism can cause loss of face and silence. Give praise in public and difficult feedback in private, start with facts rather than judgments, and ask the person for their own analysis first. Being respectful does not mean avoiding the issue: unclear feedback is unkind because people cannot fix what they have not heard.

items.label: Weekly
items.text: 15-minute huddle: yesterday's numbers, today's priorities, blockers

items.label: Monthly
items.text: One-to-one: scorecard, development, support needed

items.label: Quarterly
items.text: Unit review with your manager; reset OKRs

items.label: Annual
items.text: Appraisal, calibration across units, development plan

lessons.tip: End every one-to-one by asking: what will you do differently before we meet next, and what do you need from me?

scenario.title: The missed target
scenario.situation: Getachew Lemma, a senior relationship manager, missed his fee income target for two quarters. He says FX trade volumes fell after his two largest importers moved to another bank. In past reviews his manager only said "try harder".
scenario.question: What is the best approach in the next one-to-one?
options: Warn him in the team meeting so others learn
Say nothing and wait for the annual appraisal
Go through the facts together, ask for his analysis of why the clients left, agree two or three specific actions and a date to review
Lower his target so he feels better
scenario.explain: Private, fact-based feedback with his own analysis and specific actions gives him a real chance to recover; public criticism or silence does not.

takeaways: Strategies usually fail in execution: too many priorities, no owners, budgets and targets not linked.
A balanced scorecard adds customer, process and learning measures that predict financial results.
OKRs focus a team for a quarter on a few measurable outcomes, ideal for change initiatives.
Cascade targets by potential, agree them with unit heads and check that the parts add up to the whole.
Weights and caps make a scorecard reflect what matters most and stop one result from hiding another.
Review on a fixed rhythm, give difficult feedback privately and factually, and end with agreed actions.

quiz.q: Which is a leading indicator in a balanced scorecard?
options: Share of staff certified on the new system
quiz.explain: Learning and process measures predict future financial results; profit and ROE are lagging.

quiz.q: Which is a well-written key result?
options: Increase active mobile users from 30,000 to 45,000 by end of quarter
quiz.explain: It is a measurable outcome with a baseline, target and date.

quiz.q: A bank target of Birr 4,000 million is cascaded by potential. A region has 30% of potential. Its target is:
quiz.explain: 4,000 x 30% = Birr 1,200 million.

quiz.q: A measure has a 25% weight, target 80 and actual 72. Its weighted score (no cap issue) is:
Why cap each measure at, for example, 120% of target?
options: So that overachievement on one measure cannot hide failure on another
To make the score easier to calculate
quiz.explain: Caps keep the scorecard balanced across priorities.

quiz.q: In an Ethiopian team, the best way to give difficult feedback is usually to:
options: Raise it in the team meeting
Deliver it privately, with facts, after asking for the person's own view
quiz.explain: Private, factual feedback respects the person and still gets the message across.

modules.title: Leading major change
modules.summary: Use Kotter, ADKAR, change governance, stakeholder mapping, impact assessment and communication plans to lead mergers and system migrations.
objectives: Explain why change programs fail and use Kotter's eight steps and ADKAR to plan and diagnose
Set up change governance with clear decision rights
Map stakeholders by power and interest and plan how to engage each group
Assess change impact and build a communication plan for a merger or system migration

lessons.title: Why change fails, and Kotter's eight steps
body: Large change fails for predictable reasons: no sense of urgency, a leadership group that is not united, a vision nobody can explain, too little communication, obstacles left in place, no early wins, declaring victory too soon and new ways of working that never become "how we do things here". John Kotter's eight steps address each of these in turn.

People also move through an emotional change curve: shock and denial, then frustration and low mood, then experimenting and finally commitment. Leaders cannot skip the curve, but they can shorten it with honest information, support and early wins. Expect productivity to dip before it improves, and plan for it.

items.label: Create urgency
items.text: Show why the status quo is more dangerous than change

items.label: Build a guiding coalition
items.text: Senior leaders and respected informal leaders

items.label: Form a vision and strategy
items.text: A picture people can explain in one minute

items.label: Communicate the vision
items.text: Many times, many channels, by example

items.label: Remove obstacles
items.text: Systems, rules and people that block the change

items.label: Create short-term wins
items.text: Visible results within the first months

items.label: Build on the change
items.text: Use credibility from wins to go further

items.label: Anchor in culture
items.text: New behaviors become the norm

example.title: The tablets that stayed in the box
example.text: A bank bought tablets for paperless account opening in 60 branches. Head office sent a circular and one training video. Three months later, most branches still used paper: tellers feared the system would be slow at peak times and that errors would be blamed on them. A second rollout used branch champions, a two-week parallel run and a weekly league table of tablet use. Adoption passed 80% within two months.

lessons.tip: Plan for the productivity dip: add temporary staff or extend hours during the first weeks of a new system.

lessons.title: ADKAR: change one person at a time
body: Kotter describes what the organization must do; Prosci's ADKAR describes what each person must go through. Change happens when a person has Awareness of the need, Desire to take part, Knowledge of how to change, Ability to do it in practice and Reinforcement that makes it stick.

ADKAR is a powerful diagnostic. When a group resists, find the first element that is missing and work on that one. Training (Knowledge) does not help someone who still lacks Desire; a speech about urgency (Awareness) does not help someone who wants to change but lacks the Ability.

items.label: Awareness
items.text: Why is this change needed?

items.label: Desire
items.text: What is in it for me and my team?

items.label: Knowledge
items.text: How do I do it?

items.label: Ability
items.text: Can I actually do it on a busy day?

items.label: Reinforcement
items.text: Is it recognized and does it stick?

example.title: Diagnosing a credit team
example.text: Selamawit Desta led the move to a new loan origination system. Her credit analysts attended training but kept using spreadsheets. In interviews she found they did not see why the change was needed: the spreadsheets worked for them. She shared turnaround data showing the bank losing SME clients to faster competitors. Once Awareness and Desire were in place, usage rose without more training.

scenario.title: Trained but not using it
scenario.situation: After the core banking migration pilot, 90% of tellers at the Mekelle branch passed the system test, but they still keep a paper log of every transaction "just in case".
scenario.question: Which ADKAR element is most likely missing?
options: Ability and Reinforcement: confidence on live days and signals that the old way is no longer needed
scenario.explain: They know the system (Knowledge) but lack confidence in practice and no one has removed the old habit. Floor support and a clear end to the paper log will help.

lessons.title: Change governance: who decides what
body: A merger or system migration involves hundreds of decisions. Without clear governance, decisions are made twice, not at all, or by whoever shouts loudest. A typical structure has a steering committee of senior executives, a transformation office that plans and tracks the program, workstreams with named leads, and change champions in branches and departments.

Write down decision rights: which decisions the steering committee keeps (for example, organization structure and branch closures), which the transformation office can make (sequencing, resource moves within budget) and which workstreams decide alone. Set a fixed rhythm: weekly workstream reports, a fortnightly steering committee and a red, amber, green dashboard of milestones and risks.

items.label: Board
items.text: Approves the merger plan and major structure decisions

items.label: Steering committee
items.text: CEO and senior executives; decides escalated issues

items.label: Transformation office
items.text: Plans, tracks, manages risks and dependencies

items.label: Workstreams
items.text: IT, operations, HR, customers, risk, finance, branding

items.label: Change champions
items.text: One per branch or department; voice of the front line

example.title: Andinet's transformation office
example.text: Hirut Alemu's office has eight people: herself, a program planner, a risk and dependency manager, a change and communication lead, an HR integration lead and three workstream coordinators. Each of seven workstreams has one lead from Bank A and one deputy from Bank B, which signals that the merger is a joining of equals. The steering committee, chaired by the designated CEO, meets every second Tuesday.

scenario.title: Two banks, two answers
scenario.situation: The IT workstream wants to freeze all system changes for six months; the customer workstream wants to launch a joint mobile app in month three. Both leads say the decision is theirs.
scenario.question: Who should decide?
options: Each bank decides for its own customers
The transformation office analyzes the trade-off and the steering committee decides, since it affects two workstreams and the customer plan
scenario.explain: Cross-workstream conflicts with customer impact belong to the steering committee, supported by the transformation office's analysis.

lessons.title: Stakeholder mapping and engagement
body: Stakeholders are people and groups who affect or are affected by the change. A power and interest grid sorts them into four groups: manage closely (high power, high interest), keep satisfied (high power, lower interest), keep informed (lower power, high interest) and monitor (lower power and interest).

For a bank merger the list is long: shareholders and boards of both banks, the NBE, staff and their associations, branch managers, large corporate clients, depositors, the core banking vendor, correspondent banks and the communities where branches close. Engagement means a named owner, a message and a channel for each group, not just a list.
lessons.tip: Review the stakeholder map every month; power and interest shift as the program moves.

scenario.title: The quiet shareholder
scenario.situation: A Bank B shareholder group holding 8% has not attended any briefings. Hirut hears they are unhappy about the proposed share exchange ratio and may vote against the merger.
scenario.question: What should the transformation office do?
options: Send them the standard staff newsletter
Ignore them, since they hold under 10%
Move them to manage closely: arrange a meeting with the chair and CFO to explain the valuation and listen to concerns
scenario.explain: Power can change quickly. A group that can block the vote needs direct, senior engagement.

worked.title: Andinet stakeholder map (scores 1 to 5)

rows.label: Bank B influential shareholders: power 5, interest 5
rows.value: Manage closely: CEO and chair meet monthly

rows.label: National Bank of Ethiopia: power 5, interest 4
rows.value: Manage closely: regular updates through the compliance head

rows.label: Top 200 corporate clients: power 4, interest 4
rows.value: Manage closely: named relationship manager calls before announcement

rows.label: Staff association: power 3, interest 5
rows.value: Keep informed and consult: HR lead meets fortnightly

rows.label: Core banking vendor: power 4, interest 2
rows.value: Keep satisfied: contract and milestone reviews

rows.label: Retail depositors: power 2, interest 3
rows.value: Keep informed: SMS, branch notices, call center

rows.label: Local communities where branches merge: power 2, interest 3
rows.value: Keep informed: town meetings and notices

worked.note: Every group has an owner and a channel; the four manage-closely groups get senior attention every month.

lessons.title: Change impact assessment
body: A change impact assessment asks, for every group, what will be different: processes, systems, roles, reporting lines, location, workload and culture. Rate each high, medium or low. The result tells you where to focus training, communication and support, and where the risk to customers is greatest.

Do it early and with people from the affected groups. Head office often underestimates the change for branches and overestimates it for itself. In a core banking migration, tellers and back office staff usually carry the highest impact, while customers mainly notice new account numbers, cards and channels.

scenario.title: Where to put the training budget
scenario.situation: The training budget covers 1,500 places before cutover. Bank B tellers and back office total 1,150 staff; Bank A managers want 600 places for a leadership course.
scenario.question: What is the best allocation?
options: Give Bank B tellers and back office their 1,150 places first and use the remaining 350 for relationship managers and super-users
Train only branch managers and let them cascade
Split equally between the two banks
scenario.explain: The impact assessment shows where the risk sits. Front-line Bank B staff must be ready on cutover day.

worked.title: Core banking migration: impact by group (1 low to 3 high)

rows.label: Bank B tellers (850): process 3, system 3, role 1, location 1
Bank B back office (300): process 3, system 3, role 2, location 2
Bank A tellers (1,900): process 1, system 1, role 1, location 1
Relationship managers, both banks (400): process 2, system 2, role 2, location 1
Bank B retail customers (1.1 million): new account numbers, cards and app
Conclusion
rows.value: Train Bank B tellers and back office first; plan customer communication 60 days before cutover

worked.note: Because Andinet moves to Bank A's system, the impact falls mostly on Bank B people and customers.

lessons.title: Communication plans for big change
body: A communication plan sets who hears what, when, from whom and through which channel. Sequence matters: leaders and managers hear first so they can answer questions, then staff, then customers and the public, all within hours to avoid leaks. Face-to-face messages from line managers are trusted most.

In Ethiopia, rumors travel fast through social media and messaging groups. Fill the information gap before it fills itself: tell people what you know, what you do not know yet and when they will hear more. Use Amharic and the main regional languages, and give branch managers a short question and answer sheet.

items.label: Day 0, 8:00
items.text: Board and steering committee confirm the announcement

items.label: Day 0, 9:00
items.text: Senior managers briefed with question and answer sheet

items.label: Day 0, 11:00
items.text: All staff: CEO video and branch meetings led by managers

items.label: Day 0, 14:00
items.text: Top clients called by relationship managers

items.label: Day 0, 16:00
items.text: Public statement, website, SMS to customers

items.label: Weeks 1 to 4
items.text: Weekly updates, open forums, a question line for staff

lessons.tip: Tell staff what you do not know yet and when you will know; it builds more trust than a polished message.

scenario.title: The leak
scenario.situation: On a Sunday evening, a message claiming that "40 Bank B branches will close and staff will be fired" spreads in staff groups. The official announcement is planned for Wednesday.
scenario.question: What should the transformation office recommend?
options: Bring forward a short, honest message on Monday morning: what is decided, what is not, and when staff will hear more, delivered through managers
Wait for Wednesday so the plan is not disturbed
Ask staff to leave the messaging groups
scenario.explain: Silence lets rumors set the story. A quick, honest message through trusted managers restores credibility even before all decisions are made.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/93/2025, Recovery plans
regulation.text: In force since 13 May 2025 and issued under Proclamation No. 1360/2025, it requires every bank to keep a recovery plan with indicators and triggers, scenario analysis, recovery options and contingency and communication plans, approved by the board and updated annually. A merger changes the bank's structure, so the combined bank's plan, including its communication plan, should be refreshed as part of integration.

takeaways: Change fails for predictable reasons; Kotter's eight steps address them in order.
Use ADKAR to find the first missing element for each group and fix that one.
Clear governance and written decision rights prevent decisions from being made twice or not at all.
Map stakeholders by power and interest, and give each group an owner, a message and a channel.
A change impact assessment shows where to focus training and support; in a migration it is usually the side changing systems.
Sequence communication so managers hear first, and fill the information gap before rumors do.

quiz.q: Which is Kotter's first step?
quiz.explain: Without urgency, people see no reason to leave the status quo.

quiz.q: Staff understand why change is needed and want it, but cannot yet use the new system confidently. In ADKAR terms, what is missing?
quiz.explain: Knowledge has been taught but Ability, doing it in practice, still needs coaching and practice.

quiz.q: A stakeholder with high power and low interest should usually be:
quiz.explain: High power, lower interest stakeholders are kept satisfied so they do not become blockers.

quiz.q: Who should normally decide a conflict between two workstreams that affects customers?
options: The steering committee, with analysis from the transformation office
quiz.explain: Cross-workstream decisions with customer impact are escalated.

quiz.q: When merging onto Bank A's core system, which group usually carries the highest change impact?
options: Bank B tellers and back office
quiz.explain: The side changing systems faces the largest process and system change.

quiz.q: What does SBB/93/2025 require recovery plans to include?
options: Indicators and triggers, scenario analysis, recovery options, and contingency and communication plans
quiz.explain: These are the elements the directive lists, with board approval and annual updates.

modules.title: Mergers and transformation
modules.summary: Integrate two cultures, keep the people you cannot lose and restructure fairly within Ethiopian labor law.
objectives: Explain why Ethiopian banks are consolidating and why many mergers disappoint
Diagnose two organizational cultures and plan their integration
Design a talent retention plan and fair selection for the new structure
Plan restructuring and staff consultation that respects the Labour Proclamation

lessons.title: Why banks merge, and why mergers disappoint
body: Ethiopian banks face a higher bar. SBB/94/2025 sets Birr 5 billion paid-up capital for any new bank, and the minimum capital rule for existing banks, reported as SBB/78/2021, requires them to reach the same Birr 5 billion. Foreign entry under Proclamation No. 1360/2025 adds competition. For some banks, a merger is the fastest way to meet the capital rule and gain scale.

Studies of mergers worldwide find that many fail to deliver the value promised. The reasons are rarely financial: culture clash, loss of key people and customers, slow decisions and a long period of uncertainty that distracts everyone. A merger is a people program with a financial reason.

visual.caption: Running case figures: neither bank meets Birr 5 billion alone; together they do.

example.title: Capital met, customers lost
example.text: In a merger of two insurance companies, the leaders focused on the share swap and the legal steps for nine months. Staff were told little; sales teams from the smaller company left for competitors and took clients with them. The combined company met its capital target but lost about a fifth of its premium income in the first year. Its board later said the integration plan should have started on day one.

regulation.source: NBE minimum paid-up capital for banks (SBB/78/2021, as reported) and SBB/94/2025
regulation.text: The NBE's minimum capital rule for existing banks, reported as Directive No. SBB/78/2021, requires paid-up capital of Birr 5 billion, with a reported deadline of 30 June 2026. SBB/94/2025, in force since 25 June 2025, sets the same Birr 5 billion for new domestic banks and foreign bank subsidiaries and branches. Check the current NBE text and any merger guidance before relying on dates.

lessons.title: Culture integration
body: Culture is "how we do things here": how decisions are made, how much hierarchy matters, how risk is treated, how customers are served and what gets rewarded. Two banks can have the same products and very different cultures. Diagnose both cultures with surveys, interviews and observation before deciding what the new culture should be.

There are three broad choices: absorb the smaller bank into the larger one's culture, keep the best of both, or build a new culture for the new strategy. Whatever the choice, say it openly. Symbols matter: who gets the top jobs, which name and logo survive, whose processes are adopted. Staff read these signals more closely than any speech.

example.title: Andinet's culture choices
example.text: Hirut's team ran a culture survey of 1,200 staff in both banks and held 30 focus groups. They proposed keeping Bank A's credit controls and Bank B's speed and closeness to SMEs, and named the target culture "careful and close". The steering committee approved three visible signals: two of the seven executive posts for Bank B leaders, a new joint brand and Bank B's SME lending process adopted bank-wide after a control review.

scenario.title: Whose way wins?
scenario.situation: Bank B branch managers can approve SME overdrafts up to Birr 2 million; in Bank A the limit is Birr 500,000 and most requests go to head office. Bank B managers fear losing their authority after the merger.
scenario.question: What is the best approach?
options: Let each former bank keep its own limits forever
Review both against risk results and the target culture, then set one limit with controls, explaining the reasons to both groups
Apply Bank A's limits everywhere because Bank A is larger
scenario.explain: A decision based on evidence and the target culture, explained openly, avoids the message that one side simply lost.

lessons.title: Retaining the people you cannot lose
body: In every merger, competitors call your best people. Identify critical talent early: people whose loss would hurt customers, revenue, systems or controls, such as top relationship managers, core banking specialists and experienced credit and risk staff. Foreign banks entering the market will want the same people.

Retention is mostly about certainty and respect: a clear role in the new structure, a manager who talks to them and visible career prospects. Money helps when tied to staying through a defined period. Select people for new posts on transparent criteria, and announce selection decisions quickly; uncertainty is the main reason good people leave.

scenario.title: The specialist with an offer
scenario.situation: Yonas Tadesse, Bank B's lead core banking engineer, receives an offer from a fintech at 40% more pay. The migration depends on him for the next nine months.
scenario.question: What should his manager do first?
options: Remind him of his contract notice period
Meet him that day, confirm his role in the merged bank's IT team, discuss a retention award tied to the migration and his career path, and involve HR
Match the salary immediately without discussion
Let him go and hire a consultant
scenario.explain: Quick, personal attention with certainty about his future addresses the real reasons people leave; money tied to the migration helps.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/89/2024, Persons with significant influence
regulation.text: It requires NBE approval of influential shareholders holding 2% or more, directors, the CEO and senior executives. For a merged bank, the new board and executive team must be cleared before they take office, so the selection timetable for top posts must allow for the approval process.

worked.title: Andinet retention plan (worked example)

rows.label: Average monthly salary of the group
Retention award: 3 months' salary, paid half at month 6 and half at month 12
Annual revenue managed by the top 60 relationship managers
Revenue at risk if 15% of them leave and take half their clients: 1,400 x 15% x 50%

worked.note: The retention budget is less than half of one year's revenue at risk, before counting the cost of replacing specialists.

lessons.title: Restructuring within Ethiopian labor law
body: Mergers often lead to transfers, new reporting lines and sometimes fewer posts. In Ethiopia these are governed by the Labour Proclamation No. 1156/2019, which covers employment contracts, transfers, termination, including reduction of workforce, notice and severance, and the role of trade unions and collective agreements. Leaders must follow its procedures with HR and legal advice; this course does not quote its articles, so check the current text for each step.

Good practice goes beyond the minimum. First look for alternatives to job losses: redeploy staff to growing areas, retrain, freeze hiring and let natural turnover reduce numbers. Where reductions remain, use objective, published selection criteria, consult staff representatives, give the notice and payments the law requires and treat every person with dignity.

items.label: Plan
items.text: Define the new structure and how many posts are needed

items.label: Alternatives
items.text: Redeploy, retrain, freeze hiring, natural turnover

items.label: Criteria
items.text: Objective, published selection criteria checked by HR and legal

items.label: Consult
items.text: Staff representatives and unions, as the law and agreements require

items.label: Decide and notify
items.text: Written notice and entitlements under the Proclamation

items.label: Support
items.text: Counseling, references, help with new jobs

scenario.title: The fastest route
scenario.situation: A director proposes telling 150 back office staff on Friday that their posts end at month-end, to "get it over with" before the core system cutover.
scenario.question: What should Hirut advise?
options: Move the staff to remote branches instead so they resign
Announce it publicly so no one is surprised
Stop: first look at redeployment into the 60 open posts and natural turnover, then follow the Labour Proclamation's procedure with HR and legal, including consultation, criteria and notice
scenario.explain: Shortcuts break the law and trust, and pushing people out through unwanted transfers is unfair. Alternatives first, then a lawful, consulted process.

regulation.text: Ethiopia's labor law governs employment contracts, transfers, termination of employment, including reduction of workforce, notice, severance and compensation, trade unions and collective agreements. Restructuring steps, selection, consultation, notice and payments must follow its procedures and any collective agreement in force; leaders should obtain HR and legal confirmation of each step against the current text.

lessons.title: Consulting staff and their representatives
body: Consultation means sharing information early enough that staff views can change the outcome. It is different from announcing a decision and asking for questions. Where a union or staff association exists, agree a schedule of meetings, what information will be shared and how feedback will be answered.

Expect hard questions: Will there be job losses? Will salaries and benefits be harmonized up or down? Who decides postings? Do not promise what you cannot keep, such as "no job losses ever". Promise process instead: fair criteria, timely information, a hearing for every concern and decisions explained in writing.

example.title: A consultation that worked
example.text: Before integrating two microfinance institutions, the HR lead, Sara Tesfaye, met the staff association every two weeks for four months. Staff suggested that loan officers choose between two postings where possible, and that salary harmonization be phased over two years. Both ideas were adopted. Voluntary departures were half the level the board had feared, and no grievance went to court.

lessons.tip: Keep a written log of every consultation meeting, the questions raised and the answers given.

scenario.title: The demand for a guarantee
scenario.situation: The Bank B staff association asks Andinet's leaders to sign a written guarantee of "no job losses and no transfers for five years" before it supports the merger.
scenario.question: What is the best response?
options: Refuse to meet the association again
Decline the blanket guarantee but offer commitments you can keep: redeployment first, published criteria, consultation on every change and a joint review committee
Tell them the NBE has forbidden guarantees
scenario.explain: A promise the bank cannot keep destroys trust later. Firm commitments on process build durable support.

lessons.title: Running case: the 41 overlapping branches
body: In 41 towns Andinet has two branches, often on the same street. Merging them saves rent and staff costs but risks losing customers who liked their branch. Hirut's team sets decision rules: keep the better location by customer traffic and lease terms, convert the other into a service point or close it after customers have moved, and redeploy staff before any reduction.

The plan runs in three waves after the core system cutover, so customers move only once. Each wave has a clear communication plan for customers and staff, and the merged branch scorecard from module 2 tracks retention closely.

scenario.title: Which branch stays?
scenario.situation: In Debre Markos, the Bank B branch has 30% more daily customers but its lease ends in eight months; the Bank A branch has a long lease in a quieter street.
scenario.question: What should the team recommend?
options: Keep Bank A's branch because Bank A is larger
Try to renew Bank B's lease since customer traffic is the main criterion, with Bank A's site as the fallback, and decide by month four
Close both and go fully digital
scenario.explain: Applying the stated criteria, customer traffic first, keeps decisions fair and protects retention; the fallback limits risk.

worked.title: Branch consolidation: staffing effect (worked example)

rows.label: Staff in the 41 overlapping pairs today
Staff needed in 41 merged branches at 22 each
Posts no longer needed in these branches
Transfers to 18 new branches in growth towns at 12 each
Moves into the contact center and digital onboarding team
Remaining posts at risk after alternatives
rows.value: None, with about 18 roles of headroom

worked.note: Planning redeployment before announcing branch mergers removes the need for reductions in the branch network.

takeaways: Capital rules and foreign entry push Ethiopian banks toward consolidation; mergers succeed or fail on people, not on the share swap.
Diagnose both cultures, choose the target culture openly and watch the symbols staff will read.
Identify critical talent early and give them certainty quickly; money helps when tied to staying.
Restructuring must follow the Labour Proclamation No. 1156/2019, with alternatives to job losses first.
Consult early enough to change outcomes, and promise fair process rather than guarantees you cannot keep.
Plan redeployment before announcing branch consolidation.

quiz.q: Bank A has Birr 3.4 billion paid-up capital and Bank B Birr 2.1 billion. By how much does the combined bank exceed Birr 5 billion?
quiz.explain: 3.4 + 2.1 = 5.5; 5.5 minus 5.0 = Birr 0.5 billion.

quiz.q: Which is the most common reason mergers fail to deliver value?
options: People issues: culture clash, loss of key staff and customers, slow decisions
quiz.explain: Most merger failures come from integration and people, not the financial logic.

quiz.q: Under SBB/89/2024, who needs NBE approval?
options: Influential shareholders of 2% or more, directors, the CEO and senior executives
quiz.explain: These persons with significant influence need NBE approval.

quiz.q: Which is the best first step when a merger creates surplus posts?
options: Look for redeployment, retraining, hiring freezes and natural turnover
quiz.explain: Alternatives to job losses come first, before any lawful reduction process.

quiz.q: Retention awards of 2 months' salary for 100 staff earning Birr 60,000 a month cost:
quiz.explain: 100 x 60,000 x 2 = Birr 12 million.

quiz.q: Real consultation means:
options: Announcing the decision and taking questions
Sharing information early enough that staff views can change the outcome
Sending a survey after the decision
quiz.explain: Consultation must be able to influence the decision.

modules.title: Leading people, decisions and the capstone roadmap
modules.summary: Coach, lead inclusively, decide well and ethically under pressure, and present Andinet's 12-month change roadmap.
objectives: Coach team members with the GROW model and use emotional intelligence in difficult moments
Build inclusive, high-performing teams, including women and staff of different generations
Recognize decision biases, set decision rights and lead ethically under pressure
Build and present a 12-month change roadmap and plan a small real change in your own unit

lessons.title: Coaching with GROW
body: Coaching helps people find their own answers, which builds capability and commitment. It suits experienced staff facing new situations, which is exactly what change creates. The GROW model gives a simple structure for a 20-minute coaching conversation.

Ask more than you tell. Good coaching questions are open: What would success look like? What have you tried? What else could you do? What will you do first, and by when? Save direct instruction for urgent or high-risk situations and for new staff who need it, in line with situational leadership.

items.label: Goal
items.text: What do you want to achieve?

items.label: Reality
items.text: What is happening now? What have you tried?

items.label: Options
items.text: What could you do? What else?

items.label: Will
items.text: What will you do, by when, and how will I know?

example.title: Coaching a new merged-branch manager
example.text: Lidya Mekonnen, from Bank B, now manages the merged Hawassa branch with 22 staff from both banks. She told her regional manager the two groups sat apart and did not help each other. Instead of giving advice, he asked GROW questions. Lidya chose to mix teller pairs across the former banks, start a joint morning huddle and ask one person from each side to co-lead the customer migration desk. A month later, the branch's retention score rose.

scenario.title: Coach or tell?
scenario.situation: On cutover weekend, a teller calls her supervisor because the new system is rejecting a cash deposit and a long queue is forming.
scenario.question: What should the supervisor do?
options: Tell her to figure it out
Give clear direct instructions and the escalation route now, and coach on it later
scenario.explain: Urgent, high-risk moments call for direction; coaching fits when there is time to learn.

lessons.title: Emotional intelligence and wellbeing in change
body: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize and manage your own emotions and to read and respond to others'. Daniel Goleman describes five parts: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skill. In a merger, staff watch the leader's mood closely; a calm, honest leader steadies the whole team.

Long change programs strain people. Watch for signs of overload: more sick days, mistakes, irritability, people working late every night. Protect wellbeing by setting realistic workloads during cutovers, rotating peak shifts, recognizing effort and making it normal to ask for help. Wellbeing is part of performance, not separate from it.

items.label: Self-awareness
items.text: Know your triggers and your effect on others

items.label: Self-regulation
items.text: Stay calm and fair under pressure

items.label: Motivation
items.text: Keep purpose when results are slow

items.label: Empathy
items.text: Understand what the change means for each person

items.label: Social skill
items.text: Build trust across both former banks

example.title: A leader who noticed
example.text: During the migration of a bank's loan system, Tewodros Bekele saw that his best analyst had stopped joking and was making small errors. In a private conversation she said she was caring for a sick parent and working past midnight on data cleansing. He moved part of her work to two colleagues for a month and arranged flexible hours. She stayed, and the data work finished on time.

lessons.tip: Ask "How are you finding this?" in every one-to-one during a big change, and listen to the answer.

lessons.title: Inclusive leadership, women in leadership and generations
body: Inclusive teams make better decisions because they see more options and risks. Inclusion means everyone can contribute and progress: women and men, staff from different regions and languages, and different generations. SBB/91/2024 requires at least two women on every bank board, a signal that leadership balance is now a governance matter.

Practical steps: track representation at each level, make selection panels mixed, use clear criteria for promotion, offer mentoring and flexible arrangements, and stop meetings from being dominated by a few voices. Generations differ too: younger staff often expect fast feedback and digital tools, while experienced staff bring client relationships and judgment. Pair them so each learns from the other.

scenario.title: The selection panel
scenario.situation: For 41 merged-branch manager posts, the first shortlist has 3 women among 60 candidates, although 38% of supervisors are women. All panel members are men from Bank A.
scenario.question: What should HR and the transformation office do?
options: Review the shortlisting criteria for hidden bias, invite qualified women supervisors to apply, and form mixed panels from both banks
Delay all appointments by a year
Proceed, since the shortlist followed the process
scenario.explain: A sharp drop between pipeline and shortlist suggests the process, not the talent, is the issue. Fair criteria and mixed panels address it without quotas on individual posts.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/91/2024, Bank corporate governance
regulation.text: Every bank board must have at least nine directors, one-third of them independent and at least two women, with no director serving more than six consecutive years. The rule applies to the board, but it signals the NBE's expectation that banks build a balanced leadership pipeline below board level too.

worked.title: Andinet women in leadership pipeline (worked example)

rows.label: Target for the merged structure
rows.value: At least 25% of branch manager posts within two years

worked.note: The pipeline narrows sharply at branch manager level, so mentoring and fair selection for merged-branch posts are where action pays off.

lessons.title: Decision-making: biases and decision rights
body: Leaders under pressure fall into predictable biases: confirmation bias (seeking evidence that supports what we already believe), anchoring (sticking to the first number heard), overconfidence, groupthink (agreeing to keep harmony), sunk cost (continuing because we have already spent a lot) and status quo bias. Respect for hierarchy can strengthen groupthink.

Counter them with process: ask someone to argue the opposite case, gather views before the senior person speaks, set kill criteria for projects in advance and write down the reasons for big decisions. Clear decision rights, such as a RACI chart showing who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed, stop decisions from being delayed or reopened.

items.label: Confirmation
items.text: Seek evidence against your view

items.label: Anchoring
items.text: Build estimates from several starting points

items.label: Groupthink
items.text: Ask juniors first, assign a challenger

items.label: Sunk cost
items.text: Judge only future costs and benefits

items.label: Status quo
items.text: Compare the cost of doing nothing

scenario.title: Throwing good money after bad
scenario.situation: Bank B has spent Birr 90 million on a half-finished upgrade of its own core system. The merger plan moves all accounts to Bank A's system. A Bank B executive argues that finishing the upgrade for Birr 40 million more is wise "because we have already invested so much".
scenario.question: What is the soundest view?
options: Finish it to protect the Birr 90 million
Split the difference and spend Birr 20 million
Treat the Birr 90 million as sunk; compare only the future Birr 40 million against its future benefit, which is small if accounts move to Bank A's system
scenario.explain: Past spending cannot be recovered. Only future costs and benefits should drive the decision.

lessons.title: Ethical leadership under pressure
body: Change brings pressure to cut corners: hitting migration deadlines by skipping reconciliations, pushing products to meet aggressive targets, favoring friends in selection for new posts, or keeping bad news from the board. Ethical leaders set the example: they keep controls in place, give honest reports and make fair decisions even when it is costly.

A simple test helps: Would I be comfortable if this decision were reported to the board, the NBE and my family? Is it fair to everyone affected? Does it follow the law and the bank's policies? If any answer is no, stop and escalate. Protect people who raise concerns; in a hierarchical culture, staff speak up only if they see it is safe.

example.title: The reconciliation that delayed cutover
example.text: Two days before a planned cutover, Fikru Demissie, head of operations, found that 1,400 Bank B accounts did not reconcile with the migrated balances. The deadline had been announced publicly. He recommended a one-week delay to the steering committee and explained the risk to customers. The committee agreed, the issue was fixed, and no customer complaint about wrong balances followed. His credibility rose, not fell.

lessons.tip: Write down the reasons for a hard ethical call at the time; it protects you and teaches others.

scenario.title: Pressure to hit the number
scenario.situation: To show early merger wins, a regional director asks branch managers to open accounts for customers' relatives without their full KYC documents, "to be completed later", so the new-customer target is met this quarter.
scenario.question: What should a branch manager do?
options: Decline, explain the KYC and reputational risk, and escalate through the proper channel if the pressure continues
Comply, since the director is senior
Open the accounts but keep a private list
scenario.explain: Incomplete KYC breaks rules and creates real risk. Declining and escalating protects customers, the bank and the manager.

lessons.title: Capstone: the 12-month Andinet roadmap
body: As Andinet's transformation office, your team presents a 12-month change roadmap to the steering committee. It brings together everything in this course: the strategic case and scenarios (module 1), the scorecard and targets (module 2), governance, stakeholders, impact and communication (module 3), culture, talent and fair restructuring (module 4) and leadership of people and decisions (module 5).

The roadmap is assessed as 40% of the course grade, the test as 30%, a work assignment as 20% and participation as 10%. For the work assignment, lead a small real change in your own unit, for example moving a paper process to a digital one, and report what you did, which tools you used, what worked and what you would change.

items.label: Months 1 to 2
items.text: Governance set up, culture diagnostic, top team selected and NBE approvals sought, Day 0 announcement

items.label: Months 3 to 4
items.text: Critical talent retained, organization design, staff consultation, customer communication plan

items.label: Months 5 to 7
items.text: Bank B staff trained, data cleansing, mock migrations, legal merger steps completed

items.label: Month 8
items.text: Core banking cutover on a long weekend, with floor support in every branch

items.label: Months 9 to 11
items.text: Three waves of branch consolidation, joint brand launched, redeployment

items.label: Month 12
items.text: Benefits review, culture pulse survey, lessons learned, handover to business as usual

scenario.title: The steering committee's first question
scenario.situation: During your capstone presentation, the designated CEO asks: "If you could protect only one thing in the first 12 months, what would it be?"
scenario.question: Which answer is best supported by the course?
options: Customers and the people who serve them: retention of key clients and critical staff through a stable cutover
scenario.explain: Merger value is lost mainly through lost customers and people. Savings follow only if the core business holds.

worked.title: Roadmap checklist for the capstone presentation

rows.label: Case for change and vision
rows.value: One page, linked to the four scenarios

rows.label: Governance
rows.value: Steering committee, transformation office, workstreams, decision rights

rows.label: Stakeholder plan
rows.value: Map with owners and channels for each group

rows.label: Change impact and training
rows.value: By group, with Bank B front line first

rows.label: People plan
rows.value: Culture, retention, selection, consultation, Labour Proclamation steps

rows.label: Milestones and KPIs
rows.value: Monthly milestones; retention, migration accuracy, mobile adoption

rows.label: Top five risks
rows.value: Each with owner, early warning sign and response

worked.note: A roadmap that covers these seven parts, with owners and dates, is ready for the steering committee.

takeaways: Coach with GROW when there is time to learn; give direct instruction in urgent, high-risk moments.
Emotional intelligence and attention to wellbeing keep people performing through long change.
Inclusive leadership is measurable: track the pipeline, fix selection and mix panels and teams.
Counter biases with process: challengers, juniors first, kill criteria and written reasons; set clear decision rights.
Ethical leaders keep controls and honesty when deadlines press, and protect those who speak up.
A strong 12-month roadmap joins strategy, governance, stakeholders, people and risks, with owners and dates.

quiz.q: In GROW, what does the "W" stand for?
options: Will: what the person will do and by when
quiz.explain: Will turns options into a commitment with a date.

quiz.q: Which component of emotional intelligence is about understanding what the change means for each person?
quiz.explain: Empathy is reading and responding to others' feelings and situations.

quiz.q: Women are 38% of supervisors but 15% of branch managers. What does this most likely show?
options: A pipeline blockage at the step to branch manager that selection and development should address
quiz.explain: The sharp drop at one step points to the promotion process.

quiz.q: Continuing a project because of what has already been spent is:
quiz.explain: Only future costs and benefits should drive the decision.

quiz.q: Under SBB/91/2024, how many women must a bank board have at least?
quiz.explain: The directive requires at least two women directors.

quiz.q: In the capstone assessment, what weight does the change roadmap carry?
quiz.explain: Roadmap 40%, test 30%, work assignment 20%, participation 10%.

exam.q: Andinet's strategy team finds that a mobile channel pays off in all four scenarios, while 30 new branches pay off in only one. How should the roadmap treat them?
options: Fund neither until the merger closes
Fund mobile now as a no-regret move and stage branch openings against signposts
Fund branches first because customers like branches
exam.explain: No-regret moves go ahead; bets that work in only some futures wait for signposts.

exam.q: Which pair of forces most threatens a bank's large-corporate business after foreign entry and the launch of the securities exchange?
options: Customer power of small savers and technology
Supplier power and rivalry from MFIs
exam.explain: Foreign banks are new entrants and capital market funding is a substitute for corporate loans.

exam.q: A department head's team never disagrees with her in meetings. What is the best change in a hierarchical culture?
options: Ask juniors for written views first and have the most junior person present first
Ask only senior staff for opinions
exam.explain: Structured ways to speak before the leader reduce deference and surface risks.

exam.q: The NBE raised the National Bank Rate at MPC meeting No. 7 in July 2026 to:
exam.explain: The rate rose by one point to 16%; 13.4% was reported headline inflation in May 2026.

exam.q: A measure has a 20% weight, target Birr 50 million and actual Birr 70 million, with a 120% cap. Its weighted score is:
A bank target of Birr 9,000 million is cascaded; a region has 22% of potential and a branch has 10% of that region's potential. The branch target is:
Which OKR key result is strongest for a digital onboarding objective?
options: Raise share of accounts opened digitally from 20% to 60% by quarter end with return rate below 2%
exam.explain: It is an outcome with a baseline, target, date and a quality guard.

exam.q: A branch scorecard has only financial measures. What is the main risk?
options: Problems with customers, processes and people show up only after results fall
exam.explain: Without leading indicators, the manager gets no early warning.

exam.q: Tellers who passed the system test still keep paper logs after go-live. Using ADKAR, which action fits best?
options: Explain the merger's strategic rationale again
Provide floor support on live days, confirm the paper log is no longer needed and recognize staff who stop it
exam.explain: The gap is Ability and Reinforcement, not Awareness or Knowledge.

exam.q: Which item belongs to the steering committee rather than a workstream?
options: Whether a joint mobile app launches before cutover, delaying the IT freeze
The format of a weekly report
The order of data cleansing tasks
exam.explain: Cross-workstream trade-offs with customer impact are escalated.

exam.q: A Bank B shareholder group with enough votes to block the merger shows rising concern. Where does it sit on the power and interest grid?
exam.explain: High power and now high interest means senior, direct engagement.

exam.q: Rumors of branch closures spread three days before the announcement. The best response is to:
options: Stay silent until the planned date
Issue a short, honest message through managers on what is and is not decided and when staff will hear more
exam.explain: Filling the information gap quickly restores trust.

exam.q: Under SBB/93/2025, recovery plans must be:
options: Approved by the CEO only, every three years
Approved by the board and updated annually
exam.explain: The directive requires board approval and an annual update.

exam.q: Bank A's paid-up capital is Birr 2.8 billion and Bank B's is Birr 1.9 billion. To reach Birr 5 billion after merging, they must still raise:
exam.explain: 2.8 + 1.9 = 4.7; 5.0 minus 4.7 = Birr 0.3 billion.

exam.q: Before the merged bank's new CEO and directors take office, what does SBB/89/2024 require?
options: NBE approval of directors, the CEO and senior executives
exam.explain: Persons with significant influence need NBE approval.

exam.q: Which restructuring step order best fits the Labour Proclamation No. 1156/2019 and good practice?
options: Notify, then consult, then look for alternatives
Plan, look for alternatives, set objective criteria, consult, notify with legal entitlements, support
exam.explain: Alternatives and consultation come before lawful notice; pushing people out by transfer is unfair.

exam.q: The 41 overlapping branches have 1,230 staff and need 902. Redeployment covers 216 to new branches and 70 to digital teams, and natural turnover is about 60. How many posts remain at risk?
A Bank B executive wants to spend Birr 40 million to finish an upgrade of a system that will be retired, because Birr 90 million is already spent. This reflects:
exam.explain: Past spending is sunk; only future value matters.

exam.q: A regional director asks branches to open accounts without full KYC to show early merger wins. The ethical response is to:
options: Decline, explain the risk and escalate through proper channels
Open accounts only for relatives of staff
exam.explain: Breaking KYC rules to hit targets creates legal and reputational risk.

exam.q: Your capstone roadmap is strong on systems and legal steps but has no stakeholder plan or people plan. Based on the course, what is the main weakness?
options: Nothing: systems are the hardest part
It ignores the people and customer risks that cause most merger failures
exam.explain: Mergers fail mainly on culture, talent and customers, so these parts are essential.
